summary: This standards-track memo defines the Content-Disposition header field for MIME messages, which conveys presentation information such as whether a body part should display inline or be treated as an attachment.

plainLanguage.summary: The Content-Disposition header tells a mail program how the sender wants a message part presented. It can mark a part for display with the message or as an attachment that needs a user action.

questions: how does the filename parameter work in mime
is it safe to trust the content-disposition filename
what is the difference between inline and attachment
subtitle: A MIME header that suggests whether a message part should display inline or as an attachment.

tldr.problem: MIME describes message parts but leaves their presentation to the mail program. Senders need a way to suggest whether a part should display with the message or be opened separately.
tldr.mechanism: The optional Content-Disposition header marks a part as inline or attachment and can include a filename, dates or approximate size.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2183 revises RFC 1806 and has been updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231, which address long or non-ASCII parameter values.

today: RFC 2183 is a Proposed Standard that revises RFC 1806. It has been updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231, which address parameter value encoding.

sections.title: Why a Presentation Header Is Needed
sections.content:
MIME packages data in Internet messages but does not specify how a mail program should present each part. A message can show parts inline as it is displayed, or keep them separate as attachments that require an action from the recipient.

The optional Content-Disposition header lets a sender indicate the intended presentation for a message or body part. It can also suggest a filename and carry file-date information.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME carries message parts but does not say how a mail program should show them. Content-Disposition lets the sender suggest a presentation.

sections.title: Header Types and Parameter Values
sections.content:
The field contains a disposition type followed by optional semicolon-separated parameters. The types defined here are inline and attachment; extension types are also allowed. Type values are not case-sensitive. If the field is absent, the mail program chooses how to present the part.

A short parameter value of 78 characters or fewer should use a plain token if it contains no special characters, or a quoted string if it contains ASCII special characters. A longer or non-ASCII value must use the encoding specified by RFC 2184.
sections.plainLanguage: The header starts with a type and can include extra details after semicolons. Long or non-ASCII values need the encoding rules named by the RFC.

sections.title: Inline Parts and Attachments
sections.content:
A part marked inline is intended to display automatically with the message, in the order the parts occur. A part marked attachment is separate from the main message and should wait for the user to request it.

On a multipart entity, the header applies to the multipart as a whole. If the multipart is inline, its parts are displayed normally except for any subpart marked as an attachment. If the multipart is an attachment, the user must first choose to display it, after which the subparts' own dispositions apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Inline parts display with the message. Attachments wait for the user, and a multipart part applies its instruction to the group it contains.

sections.title: Filename, Dates and Size
sections.content:
The filename parameter suggests a name if the recipient saves a part as a file. A mail program should check that the name fits local rules, does not overwrite an existing file and is not a security risk. It should ignore directory paths in the suggested name and treat it only as a filename component.

The creation-date, modification-date and read-date parameters can carry file dates. The size parameter gives an approximate size in octets. A filename does not require the mail program to save the part.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can suggest a filename and include file dates or an approximate size. The receiving program must check the suggested name before using it.

sections.title: Unknown Types and Nested Messages
sections.content:
Mail programs should ignore parameters they do not recognize. They should treat an unknown disposition type as attachment, so the part is not displayed automatically. Unless a parameter's definition says otherwise, parameters apply to all disposition types.

New disposition types are defined through Internet standards-track documents or approved Experimental documents. New parameters use the registration process described in the RFC. A Content-Disposition field may also appear on the main body of a message.
sections.plainLanguage: A program ignores unfamiliar parameters and treats an unfamiliar type as an attachment. The RFC also sets rules for defining new types and parameters.

sections.title: Treat Suggested Filenames as Untrusted
sections.content:
A sender can choose the value of a suggested filename, so a receiving mail program must check it before saving a part. The RFC lists risks such as overwriting a file, creating a startup file, placing an executable in a command search path or sending the file to a pipe.

The program should not name or place a file so it runs or is interpreted without the user explicitly starting that action. The examples are not exhaustive; implementers must consider hazards on their own systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A suggested filename can be unsafe. The receiving program should check it and must not cause a file to run without the user's action.
